prompt: Three tests each wait for a button that a rename removed, and the default test timeout is 30 seconds. Run with one worker, how many seconds does the run spend before it reports all three failures?
After the button became *Add to cart*, the three duplicated tests failed although the shop worked. What was actually wrong?

choices.text: Each test held its own copy of one fact about the markup
choices.why: Right. The fact changed once, and every copy of it failed separately; the repair is four edits in three places.

choices.text: The locators were fragile, and role and name should have been CSS classes
choices.why: Role and name are the locators lesson 2 recommends, and a class can be renamed just as easily. The locator was fine; it was written three times.

choices.text: The tests ran in parallel and saw one another's bananas
choices.why: They ran with one worker, one after another, and none of them got as far as adding anything.

choices.text: Nothing: a red suite after a markup change is a defect found
choices.why: The shop still worked, so there was no defect to find. The suite reported its own knowledge going stale.

prompt: What does a page object hold, in this lesson's sense of the pattern?

choices.text: A list of selector strings shared by the tests
choices.why: That moves the strings and keeps the problem: tests still say *click this button* and still repeat multi-step actions.

choices.text: The expected results of every test of the page
choices.why: Expectations stay in the tests; section 05 is about why.

choices.text: What a customer does on one page and sees there, with its locators
choices.why: Right. Behaviour in the customer's words, and the knowledge of where things are behind it.

choices.text: Its own browser, so that each test is isolated
choices.why: It is handed the test's `page` and starts nothing; isolation comes from the context Playwright gives each test.

prompt: With `ShopPage` in place, the button is renamed and all three tests fail again. Where do the stack traces point first?

choices.text: To the line of each test that adds a fruit
choices.why: The test's line appears too, below, as the step in progress; the first frame is where the button is named.

choices.text: To `app/public/app.js`, where the text changed
choices.why: Playwright knows nothing of the shop's source; it reports where the test code was waiting.

choices.text: Nowhere: a timeout carries no stack trace at all
choices.why: The capture shows one: the call log, then the code frame at `shop-page.js:14`, then the spec's line.

choices.text: To line 14 of `pages/shop-page.js`
choices.why: Right. `ShopPage.addToBasket` is the one place that names *Add to basket*, so one edit there makes all three pass.

prompt: A colleague worries that `basketCount()` builds a new locator on every call, before the page has drawn anything. What happens?

choices.text: It finds the element once and goes stale when the header is redrawn
choices.why: That is how a stored element handle behaves. A locator holds no element at all.

choices.text: Nothing is found until the locator is used, against the page as it is then
choices.why: Right. A locator is a description resolved at each use, so building one early or often costs nothing.

choices.text: It throws, because the count is drawn after the products arrive
choices.why: Creating a locator never looks at the page, so there is nothing to throw about yet.

choices.text: Each call slows the test, so it should be made once in the constructor
choices.why: Building a locator does no work in the browser; either place is fine.

prompt: Put the layers in order, from the one that knows least about the HTML to the HTML itself.
trap: A markup change enters at the bottom and should stop at the locators.

prompt: `ProductCard` is constructed from a root locator. What does that buy?

choices.text: Faster tests, since the card is located only once
choices.why: Locators are resolved at each use whatever they start from; the gain is scope, not speed.

choices.text: Strict mode can no longer complain about eight buttons
choices.why: Scoping does avoid the eight matches, but that is a side effect: chaining from the card did it in lesson 2 without a class.

choices.text: One class serves any card it is handed, on any page
choices.why: Right. Every locator inside starts from the root, which is why the guava card passed on `/` and on `/ssr`.

choices.text: A card can be checked without the page loading
choices.why: Every check still runs against a loaded page; the component only decides where to look in it.

prompt: A team gives every page object a `BasePage` parent holding the header. A new checkout page has no header but a progress bar. What goes wrong?

choices.text: It inherits header methods it cannot honestly offer
choices.why: Right. Holding parts as fields lets each page have exactly the parts it draws, and say so in its constructor.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the checkout page overrides the header methods
choices.why: Overriding them to do what? The page still offers a header it does not have; the class lies about the page.

choices.text: The tests fail at once, because `extends` needs every method
choices.why: JavaScript requires nothing of the kind; the inherited methods simply sit there until somebody calls one.

choices.text: The progress bar must be put into `BasePage` as well
choices.why: That is the road to every page inheriting every part; it makes the problem bigger rather than solving it.

prompt: With the basket's answer held back 200 ms, `expect(await shop.basket.itemCount()).toBe(1)` failed five times in five. Why?

choices.text: `Number()` turned the text into `NaN`
choices.why: Every failure received `0`, a number; the text was a digit, only the wrong one.

choices.text: `toBe` compares objects by reference, not by value
choices.why: For numbers `toBe` compares the values; `0` is simply not `1`.

choices.text: The route stopped the request from reaching the server
choices.why: The route delays and then continues it; the polled test, on the same route, saw the count reach 1.

choices.text: The count was read once, before the answer redrew it
choices.why: Right. `textContent()` is a snapshot, and a plain `expect` on a value never asks again.

prompt: Which version of the count lets the test keep Playwright's retrying assertions?

choices.text: `async itemCount()` returning `Number(await count.textContent())`
choices.why: That is the snapshot that failed five times in five; only a poll around it retries.

choices.text: `basketCount()` returning the locator
choices.why: Right. `expect(locator).toHaveText('1')` reads again until it matches or time runs out.

choices.text: `checkCount(n)`, with the `expect` inside the page object
choices.why: It can retry, but it hides the expectation and fits one test; the retry was never the page object's to own.

choices.text: A getter that caches the first text it reads
choices.why: Caching makes the snapshot permanent: the test would compare the count from before the click forever.

prompt: A test checks what the shop shows when its products fail to load. Its page object's `open()` ends by expecting a visible product card. What does that assertion do to this test?

choices.text: Fails it inside `open()`, before it looks at the error
choices.why: Right. This is the argument against assertions in page objects: a precondition for most tests is the subject of this one.

choices.text: Makes it more reliable, since it confirms the page opened
choices.why: It confirms the opposite of what this test sets up; the page object has decided what *loaded* means for everyone.

choices.text: Nothing, because assertions inside classes do not retry
choices.why: An `expect` on a locator retries wherever it is written.

choices.text: Passes it, since `open()` runs before the test body starts
choices.why: A failure anywhere the test awaits, in a page object or a fixture, fails the test.

prompt: To add a fixture of your own, such as `shop`, you call `test.___ ({ shop: async ({ page }, use) => { … } })` and export the result.
In the `shop` fixture, where does code that must run after the test go?

choices.text: In an `afterEach` that the fixture file exports
choices.why: A fixture carries its own cleanup; nothing outside it is needed.

choices.text: Before `use`, because the runner reverses the order
choices.why: Code before `use` is setup and runs first; nothing is reversed.

choices.text: Nowhere: fixtures cannot clean up
choices.why: `page` itself is a fixture that closes the page after each test.

choices.text: After `await use(shop)`, which returns when the test ends
choices.why: Right. The test runs while `use` waits; what follows it is the teardown.

prompt: The card tests ask for `page` and not for `shop`, in a suite where the fixtures file defines `shop`. What does the `shop` fixture do for them?

choices.text: Resets the basket first, like every other test
choices.why: Fixtures are set up on demand; a test that does not name one does not pay for it.

choices.text: Opens the shop, then their `goto` loads it again
choices.why: No page load happens on their behalf; only their own `goto` runs.

choices.text: Nothing, since they import `test` from `@playwright/test` and never name it
choices.why: Right. Neither the import nor the argument mentions it, so it is never built for them.

choices.text: Breaks them, because a spec must import the extended `test`
choices.why: Both `test` objects work side by side; the run passed all five.

prompt: Match each page-object method to what is wrong with it.

pairs.right: named after the markup, so it changes when the markup does
a wait one test needed, paid by every test
a failure turned into a value nobody may check

pairs.left: an `AppPage` with methods for every page
pairs.right: several classes pretending to be one

prompt: `basketCount()` is one line long. Why does this lesson keep it while calling `click(locator)` a wasted wrapper?

choices.text: One-line methods are fine while there are fewer than five of them
choices.why: No count decides it; the lesson names no such limit.

choices.text: Its name says what the customer sees and hides where it lives
choices.why: Right. A redesign moves the count and the name stays true; `click(locator)` only renames `locator.click()`.

choices.text: A method returning a locator cannot be a wrapper
choices.why: `getBasketCountSpan()` returns one too, and is named after the markup.

choices.text: It is used by three tests, and `click` by none
choices.why: Use counts do not rescue a name that repeats the widget; a popular wrapper is still a second vocabulary.

prompt: When does this lesson say a page object should be written?

choices.text: Before the first test, so that tests have something to call
choices.why: Written first, it guesses which steps repeat, and guesses wrong.

choices.text: When a markup change has broken a test for the first time
choices.why: Waiting for the breakage means paying for the duplication once before removing it; the signal is the repetition itself.

choices.text: Only for pages with more than one component on them
choices.why: The shop's first page object had no components at all, and earned its place.

choices.text: Once the tests repeat a step, moving only what repeats
choices.why: Right. This lesson began from three tests that repeated themselves.

prompt: The search page from lesson 3 gets a `SearchPage`. A test types `papaya` and checks the list. Which method should the page object offer for the result?

choices.text: `results()` returning the locator for `#results li`
choices.why: Right. The test can wait for `aria-busy` and then assert on the locator, which retries.

choices.text: `async resultNames()` returning the texts of the list right away
choices.why: A snapshot, read while answers are still arriving; on that page it races exactly as the count did here.

choices.text: `expectOnlyPapaya()`, which asserts inside the page object
choices.why: That hides the expectation and fits one test; the next search needs another method.

choices.text: `waitAndRead()`, sleeping a second before reading
choices.why: Lesson 3 measured that sleep: after one second it read the stale *p* answer, three fruit.

prompt: Which of these belong inside a page object or one of its components? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The test id `product-banana` and the button's accessible name
choices.why: Yes. Where things are on the page is exactly what the page object is for.

choices.text: A method `addToBasket(id)` that clicks the card's button
choices.why: Yes. An action in the customer's words, with the locators behind it.

choices.text: The expectation that two fruit make two items
choices.why: That is the test case itself, and it stays in the test where a reader can see it.

choices.text: The `POST /api/reset` that empties the basket
choices.why: Preparing the world is setup; in this lesson it lives in the `shop` fixture, not in the page.

prompt: A suite of 30 tests clicks *Add to basket* in each test, written out every time, once per test. The button is renamed. How many lines must change if the suite uses a page object whose `ProductCard` names the button?
